title: Quantum Krylov Linear Solving Beyond Global Conditioning via Spectral Compression and Directional Stability
abstract: Global condition-number dependence can substantially overestimate the difficulty of preparing normalized quantum linear-system solutions. Many existing beyond-conditioning approaches are favorable when globally ill-conditioned directions have limited relevance to the target solution. Here we study a harder regime for time-evolution quantum Krylov linear solving (QKS), where a vanishing eigenvalue remains solution-relevant and must be retained. We identify a QKS regime in which the solution-relevant spectrum is compressed into a compact reduced space where the ill-conditioning is concentrated along a soft direction aligned with the solution, so that normalization removes the divergent amplification along that direction and leaves only a bounded transverse response. Consequently, the normalized-state complexity need not inherit the divergence of the global condition number. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We show that the solution-relevant information admits a compact and stable QKS representation, with bounded subspace dimension, evolution time, and reconstruction overhead as the relevant eigenvalue vanishes. (2) We show that normalized-state difficulty is governed by whether inverse amplification changes the solution direction, rather than by the small eigenvalue alone; even an arbitrarily ill-conditioned reduced system can remain directionally stable when the amplification is solution-aligned. (3) We prove that this stability persists under finite projected-system errors and transfers to the actual QKS output, yielding an end-to-end complexity bound without inverse dependence on the retained small eigenvalue. An explicit separation family further shows that a full inverse-amplification criterion can diverge while the corresponding QKS quantities remain bounded.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes Quantum Krylov Linear Solving (QKS) for solving quantum linear systems. It demonstrates that the computational difficulty, measured by normalized-state complexity, is not dictated by the system's global condition number when a small, solution-relevant eigenvalue is present. The authors establish that the QKS method maintains stability and bounded resources even when the full system exhibits extreme spectral gaps.
main_problem: The paper addresses the overestimation of difficulty in Quantum Krylov Linear Solving (QKS) due to global condition number dependence, especially when the ill-conditioning stems from a solution-relevant, vanishing eigenvalue.
main_result: It proves that the normalized-state complexity of QKS does not need to inherit the divergence of the global condition number, even when the system is severely ill-conditioned.
method: The authors analyze the QKS process by projecting the dynamics onto a reduced, stable subspace, comparing the required resources to the full system's spectral properties.
model_or_system: The model is solving a quantum linear system $Ax = |bangle$ where $A$ is a Hermitian positive-definite operator. The solution is approximated using time-evolution states within the Krylov subspace.
key_observables: Normalized-state complexity, spectral compression stability, and the comparison between full inverse amplification ($\chi_{	ext{filt}}$) and QKS stability metrics ($K_B, K_c$).
important_parameters: The small, retained eigenvalue ($\epsilon 	o 0$), the global condition number ($\kappa(A) \sim \epsilon^{-1}$), and the Krylov subspace dimension ($m$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a solution-relevant, compact spectral representation and relies on bounding the leakage of inactive eigenvalues into the reduced subspace.
figures_summary: The notes describe the construction of explicit separation families and the analysis of embedded systems to show the divergence of full inverse amplification while QKS parameters remain bounded.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the QKS framework, then developing the core theoretical results showing bounded complexity (Theorem 1), followed by detailed analyses using spectral compression and constructing counterexamples to separate full inverse amplification from normalized-state difficulty.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical bounds for quantum algorithms solving linear systems, directly impacting the feasibility assessment of quantum simulation techniques used in AMO physics and quantum optics.
